description:
We are Team Eternal Light: three high school students who grew up looking at the Moon and wondering what it takes to land there.

We write code, build 3D worlds and dig into real NASA data. An idea isn't finished until it's checked.

Our name comes from the "peaks of eternal light": Moon summits that stay sunlit while the craters around them stay dark.

At Space Apps 2026 we built Sunchaser.
Follow the Sun. Stay in touch with Earth.
summary:
Sunchaser shows mission planners where and when to land at the Moon's south pole so a lander keeps both sunlight and contact with Earth, and it proves its numbers. We wrote the pass rules for 19 validation checks against NASA references before running them, and all 19 results, including two that failed first, are published in the app: Sun and Earth directions match JPL Horizons within 0.000002°, and sunlight at Connecting Ridge is 91.26% against 91.11% in NASA Goddard's study (Barker et al. 2021).

At the pole the Sun skims the horizon, so a ridge kilometers away can cut a lander's power for days, and the same terrain can block its link to Earth. Meters matter: in 2025, IM-2 Athena landed about 250 m off target, in a crater, and never recharged.

For the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge, Sunchaser traces the real skyline from NASA LRO LOLA terrain and places the Sun and Earth on it with NASA/JPL SPICE. For any site and hour it shows sunlight, Deep Space Network contact and the best landing windows. It compares 25 sites from Apollo to Chang'e and CLPS, checks 466,825 landing hours through 2028, replans a launch slip in one click, routes rovers through moving shadows and works anywhere on the Moon. Its 3D shadows come from the same data as its numbers, and its AI copilot cites the engine for every number.

Free in any browser, for mission planners, students and anyone who looks up.
details:
Sunchaser shows mission planners where and when to land at the Moon's south pole so a lander keeps both sunlight and contact with Earth, and it proves its numbers: 19 validation checks against NASA references, with pass rules written before running them and every result published in the app.

The problem

At the Moon's south pole the Sun never rises more than about 1.5° above a flat horizon, and Earth stays within about 7° of it. A crater rim can stay sunlit for days while the crater floor beside it stays dark, and one mountain can hide Earth. A few hundred meters decide whether a lander has power and a link to Earth, and the answer changes hour by hour. In March 2025, Intuitive Machines' IM-2 lander Athena touched down about 250 m off target, on its side in a crater about 20 m across; its panels could not face a Sun 2° above the horizon, and its power ran out the next day.

How we know it is right

We wrote the pass rule for each check before running it and published all 19 checks in the app's Validation page: 17 pass, and the 2 that failed first stay visible.

  • Sun and Earth directions vs JPL Horizons: max error 0.0000017° (pass rule: under 0.01°)
  • Sunlight at Connecting Ridge's best spot: 91.26% vs 91.11% in NASA Goddard's study (Barker et al. 2021); longest shadow 3.71 days vs 3.71 days
  • Whole-ridge sunlight vs NASA Goddard's 60 m map: correlation 0.965 over 6,889 blocks
  • Moon elevation at the Deep Space Network antennas vs JPL Horizons: max error 0.00046°
  • Rover routes 133/133 confirmed by an independent checker; copilot 151/151 numbers traced to the engine

Why those 2 failed, and the follow-up checks that pass: NASA's 60 m map is noisy on narrow crests next to the pole (the whole-map comparison above passes), and the Apollo Lunar Surface Journal's Sun-angle table proved to be a linear approximation (JPL Horizons agrees with Sunchaser to 0.0002°).

What it does

Sunchaser compares landing sites and dates by the two things a lander cannot live without: sunlight for power and line of sight to Earth for communication.

  • Explore: fly over real south-pole terrain in 3D. Drag the Sun and the computed shadows move. Click any point for its sunlight, Earth contact, a mission clock ("sunset in…", "Earthset in…") and landing slope, with links to LROC QuickMap, NASA Moon Trek and JPL Horizons.
  • Compare: 25 sites side by side (10 south-pole sites chosen by a written rule from NASA sources, plus 15 historic landings: Apollo, Chang'e, Chandrayaan-3, SLIM, CLPS) for any date, stay and panel height.
  • Landing windows: every landing hour from Nov 2026 to Dec 2028 is checked against the mission's needs. When none passes, it shows the smallest change that would open a window.
  • Replan a slip: what a launch delay does to the site, the next good date and the nearest Plan B.
  • Light Path: rover routes through moving shadows that keep the battery above its reserve (VIPER-class values).
  • Astronaut: stand on the surface and see the Sun and Earth on the real horizon.
  • Any point on the Moon: tap or type coordinates; the horizon is computed in your browser from NASA's global maps.
  • Learn, Stories and Ask Sunchaser: 15 plain-language chapters, real landings (Apollo, IM-2), and an AI copilot (English and Arabic) whose every number comes from the engine.

How it works

  • Terrain: NASA LRO LOLA elevation maps of the south pole (5–240 m per pixel); LOLA and SLDEM2015 global maps elsewhere.
  • Horizons: an exact ray walk in up to 1,440 directions finds the true skyline, including mountains hundreds of kilometers away and the Moon's curvature.
  • Sun and Earth: NASA/JPL SPICE (DE440) positions every 10 minutes, in the same lunar frame as the terrain.
  • Power: the visible fraction of the Sun's disc drives a solar-panel and battery model you can set.
  • Communication: Earth above the skyline, and the Moon at least 6° above a Deep Space Network 70 m antenna (DSN Handbook 810-005).
  • One engine: a TypeScript engine reproduces the Python pipeline (golden files agree to about 10⁻¹²), so everything runs live in the browser and the 3D shadows come from the same horizons as the numbers.

Benefits and impact

Artemis astronauts and CLPS landers are heading to the south pole. Today this analysis lives in research papers and specialist tools. Sunchaser puts it in one free app that runs on a laptop or a phone:

  • Mission planners screen sites and dates in minutes and see why a window fails.
  • Teachers and students see why a crater rim is a good landing site.
  • Anyone can stand on the surface and watch Earth rise and set.

What makes it creative

  • The real terrain horizon, computed exactly, not a flat one.
  • Sun and Earth with equal weight, down to the Deep Space Network dishes on Earth.
  • The 3D view is the analysis itself, not an illustration.
  • Every number is traceable and checked, and the failures are shown.

Limitations (stated in every view)

Terrain resolves about 20 m, so boulders and the lander itself are not modeled; Earth contact is geometric (no DSN scheduling or link budget); the solar panel is ideal; rocks in Astronaut mode are illustrative and no number uses them. Not a NASA product and not for flight operations.

Factors we considered

Accuracy before features; honest limits in every view; speed on an ordinary laptop with integrated graphics; phones; accessibility; plain language for non-experts.

Tools

TypeScript, Python, GLSL · React 19, Vite, Three.js / React Three Fiber, Web Workers · SpiceyPy (NAIF SPICE), NumPy, Numba, SciPy, rasterio · Vitest, pytest · Vercel · Google Gemini and Groq for the copilot (it also works offline).

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

We used AI tools to build Sunchaser, and we name each one here:

  • Claude Code (Anthropic): wrote most of the source code of the data pipeline and the web app under our direction, and helped with research, debugging and documentation. The science is ours: we chose the idea and the NASA datasets, designed the method (exact horizons, Sun and Earth with equal weight, the Deep Space Network rule), wrote all 19 validation pass rules before running them, tested every feature, and checked every result against JPL Horizons and NASA Goddard.
  • Google Gemini, with Groq as a backup: powers the in-app copilot "Ask Sunchaser", which only reports numbers computed by our engine and shows where they come from.
  • ElevenLabs: generated the demo video's voice-over, labeled "SI-generated: voice-over" on screen for the whole video and in the file's metadata.
  • No AI image or video generators. The video footage is real screen capture of the app plus one NASA LROC image. The three diagrams on this page and our team image were drawn with code written with Claude Code, using only the numbers in this text. No NASA branding was generated or modified.

Next steps (not built yet)

Deep Space Network scheduling, more landing sites (including the Soviet Luna landers), and faster loading on slow connections.
